# Flow-field mortality forecasting (research preview, November 2026)

Source: https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml

Samuel J. Clark · Research preview, November 2026 (replaces the [April 2026 preview](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field-2026-04.shtml))

Modern mortality forecasting follows two main traditions descended from Lee & Carter's seminal 1992 paper \[[1](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-lee-carter-1992)\]. One decomposes age-by-time mortality into a few summary patterns and projects those patterns forward. The other models how fast life expectancy improves at each level of life expectancy. We argue that both can be viewed as restricted versions of *a single underlying object*: a smooth trajectory through a low-dimensional summary of mortality derived from a multi-way decomposition of the sex × age × country × year mortality array. The unrestricted version of this object is the *flow-field forecaster*. We compare it with the leading existing methods on the Human Mortality Database \[[6](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-hmd-2024)\], with every forecast made in real time: each method sees only the data up to the year its forecast starts. The results so far are encouraging.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## How we compare forecasts

Forecasts start every five years from 1900 to 2015, for 43 populations, and run 50 years ahead. Twelve forecasters compete. The flow-field is one. MDMx, a companion forecaster built on the same decomposition, Lee–Carter \[[1](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-lee-carter-1992)\], Hyndman & Ullah's functional-data model \[[2](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-hyndman-ullah-2007)\], Hyndman, Booth & Yasmeen's coherent functional model \[[13](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-hyndman-booth-yasmeen-2013)\], and the bayesLife/MortCast pipeline \[[3](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-raftery-chunn-gerland-sevcikova-2013)\], \[[4](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-sevcikova-li-kantorova-gerland-raftery-2016)\] that the United Nations uses for its mortality forecasts \[[5](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-un-wpp-2024)\] make ten more, each fitted both to all past years and to the last 50 (bayesLife from its own Bayesian estimation at every start year). An equal-weight average of the flow-field, MDMx and Lee–Carter is the twelfth. A random walk with drift is the yardstick.

A comprehensive comparison scores each forecaster on five aspects that do not overlap: life expectancy for each sex, the gap between the sexes, the age-specific differences between the sexes, the age pattern of mortality (weighted by where deaths occur, with life expectancy at 65), and the calibration of interval forecasts. Every score measures the size of the errors, relative to the yardstick, so over- and under-predictions cannot offset each other. The forecasters are ranked over 20,000 random weightings of the five aspects, each with a resampling of the populations, so that no single choice of weights decides the result. The main test uses the forecasts from 1955–2000 at 1–15 years ahead. The forecasts from 2005–2015 were held out of every modelling choice and scored once, at the end.

## What we're seeing so far

From 1955–2000, at 1–15 years ahead, the flow-field ranks first in 90% of the 20,000 draws, ahead of the ensemble average (7%) and MDMx. Its error in life expectancy is 0.42 years at 1–5 years ahead and 0.97 years at 11–15, against 0.48 and 1.55 for the yardstick, and it is the only forecaster that beats the yardstick on every one of the nine measures. Its lead is clearest beyond five years ahead; at 1–5 years the ensemble is as accurate. On the held-out forecasts from 2005–2015 the flow-field keeps its lead, with an error of 0.25 years at 1–5 years ahead. Forecasts from the early twentieth century, outside today's regime of mortality decline, are a harder test: there the flow-field still ranks first, but in fewer than half of the draws (47%, ahead of the ensemble's 29%).

| Method | fitted to | first share of draws | rank mean, of 12 | error 1–5 years | error 11–15 years | held out 1–5 years |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | — | ↑ higher better | ↓ lower better | ↓ lower better | ↓ lower better | ↓ lower better |
| Human Mortality Database — real-time forecasts |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Flow-field | — | 90% | 1.15 | 0.42 | 0.97 | 0.25 |
| Ensemble | — | 7% | 2.73 | 0.41 | 1.09 | 0.34 |
| MDMx | all years | 1% | 3.25 | 0.49 | 1.38 | 0.29 |
| bayesLife/MortCast | last 50 | 1% | 5.20 | 0.45 | 1.34 | 0.32 |
| Coherent model | last 50 | 0% | 7.01 | 0.69 | 1.66 | 0.61 |
| Hyndman–Ullah | all years | 0% | 8.14 | 0.77 | 1.91 | 0.65 |
| Lee–Carter | last 50 | 0% | 9.93 | 0.54 | 1.20 | 0.57 |
| Random walk | all years | — | — | 0.48 | 1.55 | 0.38 |

First (share of the draws ranked first) and rank (mean rank) come from the comprehensive comparison, for the forecasts from 1955–2000 at 1–15 years ahead. Errors are mean absolute errors in life expectancy at birth (the average of the two sexes), in years, at 1–5 and 11–15 years ahead. The held-out column scores the forecasts from 2005–2015, which no modelling choice used. Each method is shown fitted to the period that serves it better (all past years, or the last 50); the ensemble averages the flow-field, MDMx and Lee–Carter; the random walk with drift is the yardstick, not a competitor.

## What this looks like as a paper

The full manuscript introduces the array-normal noise model \[[11](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-fosdick-hoff-2014)\] and the Tucker decomposition \[[7](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-tucker-1966)\] as its canonical estimator from first principles, develops the score-representation isometry that motivates a flow-on-subspace forecaster, and offers Lee–Carter, Hyndman–Ullah, and bayesLife/MortCast readings as constrained or marginal cases of the same framework — three established and successful approaches that the framework helps to relate to one another (for a recent review of Lee–Carter and its extensions, see \[[12](https://samclark.net/site/news-pages/flow-field.shtml#ref-basellini-camarda-booth-2023)\]). It then reports the real-time evaluation sketched above. The manuscript is in preparation.

*NB:* The numerical results presented here are preliminary, drawn from a manuscript in preparation. They can shift as the evaluation is refined and as the comparisons receive external scrutiny; we expect to learn a great deal from the review process. Treat what's reported here as a research preview rather than a settled comparison.

# Talks

Source: https://samclark.net/site/pages/talks.shtml

## 2025-12-12

[**Presentation**](https://samclark.net/site/talks/Sam-Clark_Reference-Data-Archive-Launch.pptx) with full RDA Team to launch the [**completed first version of the Reference Data Archive (RDA)**](https://samclark.net/site/projects/rda.shtml). \[The linked .pptx file is password protected - push the 'Read Only' button when Powerpoint asks for a password.\]

Over the past three years, I have led the creation of the [RDA](https://samclark.net/site/projects/rda.shtml) at WHO headquarter in Geneva. The RDA is a linked *trusted researcher environment* and *data catalogue/repository* designed to host sensitive data in any form, allow vetted researchers to access and analyze the data, and provide an easy-to-use and fully functional way to share both data and analytical results created with the data. Data and results shared using the RDA require acknowledgement of data providers and analysts and come with a permanent WHO-linked DOI so that they can always be located and cited.

The motivating idea behind the RDA is to provide meaningful reference datasets for training and validating methods to improve cause of death ascertainment. However, the scope is widening to include a variety of cause of death and mortality data managed and shared by WHO. Consequently, the RDA is likely to support a range of mortality-related work at WHO.

[**Talk**](https://samclark.net/site/talks/Sam-Clark_Reference-Data-Archive-Update.pptx) at the [MITS Alliance](https://mitsalliance.org/) annual meeting in Kampala Uganda describing progress on the almost-complete [**Reference Data Archive (RDA)**](https://samclark.net/site/projects/rda.shtml). \[The linked .pptx file is password protected - push the 'Read Only' button when Powerpoint asks for a password.\]
